records.name: Later dispersal out of Africa · model
records.summary: A later expansion model places movement out of Africa around 50–60 thousand years ago. Earlier dispersals and alternative northern/southern routes remain part of the debate.
records.caveat: The line is an illustrative Africa–Arabia connection, not a reconstructed itinerary. Uniform drawing progress is a visual guide, not measured travel speed or independently dated waypoints. Age estimates use 1950 only as an approximate plotting reference.

records.name: Sahul · Madjedbebe occupation
records.summary: The cited study dates an early occupation phase at Madjedbebe to approximately 65–53 thousand years ago. This is evidence at a site in Sahul, not the date of every sea crossing or a settled arrival chronology.
records.caveat: The early chronology has been discussed and challenged in the literature. The marker is an approximate site anchor; no route across Southeast Asia is inferred. OSL ages are not relabelled as calibrated radiocarbon BP; the 1950 plotting conversion is approximate.

records.name: Europe · Bacho Kiro human evidence
records.summary: The Initial Upper Palaeolithic assemblage is associated with directly dated Homo sapiens remains. The interval describes the cited archaeological context, not all human arrival in Europe.
records.caveat: Approximate cave vicinity. No exact route into Europe or uninterrupted occupation is asserted.

records.name: Americas · White Sands footprints
records.summary: Independent dating approaches support the reported footprint ages at White Sands. They establish a presence in North America; they do not identify the route, source population or first arrival on the continent.
records.caveat: Approximate park-area anchor. The dating controversy and subsequent checks are described in the source. The display uses 1950 as a reference for the rounded age interval.

records.name: Early farmers · Mediterranean to Britain
records.summary: Evidence connects British Neolithic farmers with continental populations ultimately related to Aegean farmers. The schematic links Mediterranean farming and the appearance of farming in Britain.
records.caveat: The endpoints use the cited regional chronologies. Intermediate line positions and constant animation speed are illustrative, not dates of a single population's journey. Not every British Neolithic community followed an identical route.
